question: At what dollar threshold does UC policy require competitive bidding for purchases?
ground_truth: Under BFB-BUS-43, competitive bidding is required for purchases that exceed $100,000 annually. Any purchase or aggregate spending with a supplier that surpasses this threshold must go through a competitive bidding process.
system_answer:
Answer: Competitive bid required at $100,000 or more (BUS-43: more than $100,000 annually, aggregated per supplier; CA Public Contract Code). The same $100,000 bid threshold applies to federal funds because the CA PCC is stricter than the $350,000 federal Simplified Acquisition Threshold.
Rule: Competitive bid required at $100,000 or more (BUS-43: more than $100,000 annually, aggregated per supplier; CA Public Contract Code). The same $100,000 bid threshold applies to federal funds because the CA PCC is stricter than the $350,000 federal Simplified Acquisition Threshold.
Source: BFB-BUS-43: Purchases of Goods and Services; Supply Chain Management (Interim, issued/effective January 26, 2026), p.9, III, C. Expenditures of $100,000 or More Annually, 1. General Requirements: "requires that UC competitively bid all purchases with proposed annual expenditure of $100,000 or more unless an exception applies"; FAR 2.101 Definitions (inflation adjustment, 90 FR 41872) (effective October 1, 2025), Simplified acquisition threshold: "Simplified acquisition threshold means $350,000"
Conditions: These are the general thresholds. For a determination on a specific purchase, ask with its dollar amount and funding source (federal contract, federal grant, or non-federal).

question: I'm a lab manager and I need to order reagents and lab supplies from a single vendor. I expect to place multiple orders throughout the fiscal year totaling approximately $125,000. Each individual order will be under $20,000. Do I need to go through competitive bidding?
ground_truth: Yes, competitive bidding is required. Under BFB-BUS-43, the $100,000 threshold applies to purchases on an annual aggregate basis, not per transaction. Even though each individual order is well under $100,000, the combined annual spend of $125,000 with that single vendor exceeds the $100,000 threshold, triggering the competitive bidding requirement. You should work with your procurement office to initiate a competitive solicitation before continuing to place orders with that vendor.
system_answer:
Answer: Yes, competitive bidding is required because the total annual expenditure across multiple orders with the same vendor exceeds the $100,000 competitive bid threshold. Intentionally splitting the purchase into smaller orders to avoid competitive bidding is prohibited under UC procurement policy [1].
Rule: Intentionally dividing a purchase into smaller orders to avoid bidding requirements is prohibited under BUS-43. For reference, the combined value is $125,000; the competitive bid threshold is $100,000. Competitive bid required: YES ($125,000; threshold $100,000). SSPR required: YES (threshold $100,000; sections I, VII, VIII).
Source: BFB-BUS-43: Purchases of Goods and Services; Supply Chain Management (Interim, issued/effective January 26, 2026), p.9, III, C. Expenditures of $100,000 or More Annually, 1. General Requirements: "requires that UC competitively bid all purchases with proposed annual expenditure of $100,000 or more unless an exception applies"; Source Selection & Price Reasonableness Justification Form (SSPR) (Revised 12-2025), p.1, header: "Non-Federal purchases ≥$100,000"; BFB-BUS-43: Purchases of Goods and Services; Supply Chain Management (Interim, issued/effective January 26, 2026), p.11, Solicitation, a. Competition: "UC must not artificially divide requirements into separate transactions in order to avoid competition"
Conditions: The combined annual value of $125,000 meets the $100,000 competitive bid threshold set by BUS-43 and requires competitive bidding. Additionally, an SSPR form (Sections I, VII, VIII) must be completed to document the justification for the procurement method [2].

question: Our department has been purchasing maintenance services from a vendor at $90,000 per year, which is under the $100,000 competitive bidding threshold. This year, we need to add a one-time $15,000 equipment repair from the same vendor, bringing our annual total to $105,000. Does this one-time addition push us into competitive bidding territory, even though our recurring commitment is under the threshold?
ground_truth: Yes, competitive bidding would be required. Under BFB-BUS-43, the competitive bidding threshold of $100,000 is based on total annual expenditure with a vendor, regardless of whether the spending is composed of recurring services, one-time purchases, or a combination of both. Since the combined annual spend with this vendor would reach $105,000, exceeding the $100,000 threshold, the purchase triggers the competitive bidding requirement. The department should consult with Procurement Services to determine whether a competitive solicitation is needed or whether an existing competitively bid contract can cover the expanded scope of work.
system_answer:
Answer: Yes, the one-time $15,000 addition pushes the total procurement to $105,000, which meets the $100,000 competitive bid threshold. Requirements must not be artificially divided to avoid competition, so the combined total must be treated as one procurement requiring competitive bidding.
Rule: Potential split order: $90,000 + $15,000 = $105,000. Each order is below the $100,000 competitive bid threshold but together they meet it. Requirements must not be artificially divided to avoid competition; treat this as one $105,000 procurement. Competitive bid required: YES ($105,000; threshold $100,000). SSPR required: YES (threshold $100,000; sections I, VII, VIII).

question: What is the small business set-aside exception and how many price quotes do I need?
ground_truth: The UC small business set-aside exception allows procurement from small businesses for purchases up to $250,000 without going through the full competitive bidding process. You are required to obtain a minimum of two price quotes from small business suppliers to use this exception.
system_answer:
Answer: Certified small business/DVBE: may award up to $250,000 without formal bid, any funding source. BUS-43: 1 SB/DVBE quote for $10K-$100K; 2 quotes from certified SB/DVBEs above $100K. (SSPR form federal SB option: under $100K.) BUS-43 allows small business/DVBE awards "up to $250,000" but the SSPR form says "Only <$250k"; at exactly $250,000 confirm with Procurement.

ground_truth: Yes, you can use the small business set-aside exception because your purchase of $185,000 falls within the $250,000 threshold. To proceed, you must obtain at least two price quotes from small business vendors for the lab furniture. Once you have documented those two quotes, you can award the purchase to the selected small business supplier without conducting a full competitive bid process.

question: I have a purchase for $248,000 from a small business, but I was only able to locate one other small business that provides the same product, and that vendor declined to provide a quote. Can I still use the small business set-aside exception with only one quote, or does the requirement for two price quotes mean I must find a second willing vendor?
ground_truth: The small business set-aside exception requires two price quotes. If you are unable to obtain a second quote because the only other available small business vendor declined to provide one, you likely cannot satisfy the two-quote requirement as stated in the policy. You should document your good-faith efforts to obtain the second quote and consult with your procurement office about next steps. The procurement office may advise you to pursue alternative procurement methods, seek additional small business vendors, or determine whether another applicable exception might apply. Simply having one quote does not meet the stated policy threshold of two price quotes for the small business set-aside exception up to $250,000.
system_answer:

question: When is an SSPR form required for federal purchases?
ground_truth: An SSPR (Sole Source Procurement Request) form is required for federal purchases that exceed $50,000. Any federally funded procurement over this threshold must have a completed SSPR form as part of the compliance documentation.
system_answer:
Answer: SSPR form required for: federal contract purchases >= $15,000; federal grant/cooperative agreement purchases >= $50,000; non-federal purchases >= $100,000. SSPR sections by source selection: competitive bid I, VII, VIII; federal competitive proposals (<$100K, 3 quotes per 2 CFR 200.320(a)(2)(i)) I, II, VII, VIII; federal sole source I, III, IV, VII, VIII; non-federal sole source I, III-VIII; small business/DVBE I, III, VII, VIII; professional/personal services (non-federal) I, III, V, VII, VIII; unusual & compelling urgency (non-federal) I, VI, VII, VIII. Federal micro-purchase threshold: $15,000; campuses may set up to $50,000 for grants/cooperative agreements (OMB). Simplified Acquisition Threshold: $350,000. Federally funded orders require the Federal Funds Checklist, Debarment & Suspension verification, Anti-Lobbying (Byrd) verification at $100,000+, and flow-down articles (grants: UC T&C Articles 1, 8.1(c)(i-v), 11.8, 11.9, 11.10; contracts: 8.1(a) or 8.1(b), 1, 11.10).

question: I have a federal grant and need to buy two separate pieces of equipment from the same vendor — one for $30,000 and another for $28,000. They are for related experiments in the same project. Since each individual purchase is under $50,000, do I still need to submit an SSPR form?

Each individual purchase in your scenario is below the $50,000 threshold, so on a per-transaction basis, neither would independently trigger the SSPR requirement. However, you should exercise caution: if these purchases could be reasonably viewed as a single procurement that was split to avoid the $50,000 threshold (known as order splitting), this could raise compliance concerns. The policy as stated sets the trigger at federal purchases over $50,000, so if there is any possibility the two orders could be considered a combined $58,000 procurement, you should consult your procurement office to determine whether an SSPR form is required and to ensure you are not inadvertently violating federal split-purchase prohibitions.

question: Can I break up a large purchase into smaller orders to avoid having to go through the competitive bidding process?
ground_truth: No. UC policy explicitly prohibits split-order purchasing (also known as order splitting) to avoid bidding thresholds. If a purchase reasonably constitutes a single procurement need, it must be processed as one transaction and subjected to the appropriate bidding requirements based on the total value.
system_answer: No, you cannot break up a large purchase into smaller orders to avoid having to go through the competitive bidding process. Requirements must not be artificially divided into separate transactions to avoid competition [6]. This includes prohibiting transactions that are artificially divided to falsely create multiple small Purchase Orders under the authorization limit [1].

question: Our department needs to purchase similar office furniture for three different building renovations happening at different times over the next four months, totaling $75,000. Each renovation's furniture order is about $25,000 and each has a separate project budget code. Since these are technically different projects with different funding sources and different delivery dates, can we process them as three independent purchases without triggering the competitive bid threshold?

Because the purchases involve similar goods from what would reasonably be the same vendor pool, within a relatively close timeframe, and for the same department, aggregating them into a single procurement is expected. Processing them separately to remain below the bidding threshold would violate the prohibition on split-order purchasing. The department should consult with its Procurement Services office to determine the correct approach, but the safest and most compliant path is to treat the $75,000 total as one procurement subject to competitive bidding requirements.

system_answer:

question: Under what specific condition is a sole source justification required during the procurement process?
ground_truth: A sole source justification is required when only one vendor is capable of meeting specialized research requirements.
system_answer: A sole source justification is required during the procurement process when the goods and/or services are the only ones available that will meet the University’s needs because they are unique or one-of-a-kind [1][5]. This includes situations such as emergency procurements, match existing purchases (via UC PO#), or when awarding agency approval is obtained (for federal grants and cooperative agreements) [8]. Additionally, if the procurement is federally funded and the transaction is a non-commercial contract order of $2,500,000 or more, certified cost or pricing data must be submitted as part of the sole source justification [2]. Sole source justifications must be documented in the Source Selection and Price Reasonableness Justification Form, specifically in Section IV [2][8].

question: A Principal Investigator needs a specific high-resolution microscope for a unique imaging study, and after market research, determines that no other manufacturer produces a model with the necessary technical specifications. What must the PI provide to proceed with this purchase?

system_answer: The Principal Investigator must provide a specification that includes a description of the technical features necessary to determine if other available goods are equivalent to those specified, since the use of brand or trade names should be for descriptive purposes only when no other equivalent options exist [8]. Additionally, if the microscope requires fabrication or modification, the PI must complete a Fabrication Justification Form (or University location equivalent) and submit it to the Equipment Administrator for review and approval prior to commencing any fabrication [3][4].

question: A researcher requests a sole source procurement for a specific brand of software because their existing team is already proficient in it, even though other software packages offer the same technical capabilities. Is this a valid application of the sole source policy?

system_answer: No, this is not a valid application of the sole source policy. The policy allows sole source justifications for non-federal procurements if the goods or services are "unique" or "match existing (UC PO#)" [1]. However, simply preferring a specific brand due to existing proficiency—even if other technically capable alternatives exist—does not meet the criteria for a valid sole source justification. Brand name or trade names should not be used to exclude competition unless no equivalent goods or services are available [8]. Therefore, this situation does not qualify as a valid sole source procurement under the stated policy.

question: Who is eligible for reimbursement of moving and relocation expenses according to the policy?
ground_truth: Only newly hired employees are eligible for reimbursement.
system_answer: New appointees to certain nonacademic positions requiring specialized training and/or experience of a technical, professional, or administrative nature are eligible for reimbursement of moving expenses if they reside outside the commuting distance of the campus to which they have been appointed. Additionally, current employees who are required to transfer or accept a position, including a position at the same grade or a lower grade, at a campus outside a reasonable commuting distance may be eligible for reimbursement at the campus's discretion. The move must be closely related to the start of work and meet both the time and distance tests under I.R.C. Section 217(c).2 [3].

question: An existing UC employee is transferring from the UCLA campus to the UC Berkeley campus to take on a new role. Can they request reimbursement for their moving expenses under the relocation policy?

system_answer: Yes, an existing UC employee transferring from UCLA to UC Berkeley can request reimbursement for moving expenses under the relocation policy, provided certain conditions are met. The move must be closely related to the start of work at the new location and must meet both the time and distance tests under I.R.C. Section 217(c). Specifically, the moving expenses must be incurred within one year from the time the employee first reports to the new job, and during the 12-month period following the move, the employee must be employed full-time for at least 39 weeks [1]. Additionally, the employee must reside outside the commuting distance of the UC Berkeley campus [1].
